description:
FloodLens is an interactive Earth-system trend detection platform that explores changing rainfall patterns across Pakistan using NASA satellite data and climate datasets.

It combines statistical analysis, geospatial visualisation, and machine learning to identify rainfall trends and examine regional differences.

Our goal is to make environmental changes easier to understand and support awareness, education, and further research.

FloodLens is an interactive Earth-system trend detection platform developed to investigate changing rainfall patterns across Pakistan using NASA satellite observations and climate datasets. It integrates NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data, TerraClimate variables, and geographical information into six modules: National Overview, Rainfall Explorer, Spatial Trend Explorer, Terrain Explorer, Regional Monsoon Outlook, and About & Data.

The platform applies statistical techniques, including the Mann–Kendall test, Sen's slope, and False Discovery Rate correction, to identify rainfall trends, measure their magnitude, and examine their geographical distribution. It also includes an experimental Ridge Regression model that explores relationships between pre-monsoon precipitation, soil moisture, and subsequent monsoon rainfall, with historical validation against a baseline.

FloodLens addresses NASA's "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge by transforming large environmental datasets into accessible visual evidence of how the Earth system is changing. Its goal is to support environmental awareness, education, and further research through transparent, data-driven exploration of Pakistan's rainfall patterns.
details:
FloodLens

FloodLens is an interactive Earth-system trend detection platform designed to explore changing rainfall patterns across Pakistan using NASA satellite observations, climate datasets, and geospatial analysis.

What does it do and how does it work?

FloodLens transforms environmental data into interactive maps, charts, and understandable insights. It uses NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data to examine monsoon rainfall patterns from 2001–2024, alongside TerraClimate variables such as precipitation and soil moisture. Geographical and elevation information provides additional environmental context.

The platform includes six modules: National Overview, Rainfall Explorer, Spatial Trend Explorer, Terrain Explorer, Regional Monsoon Outlook, and About & Data. Users can explore rainfall across different years and regions, examine spatial patterns, and investigate whether rainfall has increased or decreased over time.

For trend detection, we use the Mann–Kendall statistical test, Sen’s slope, and False Discovery Rate correction. We also developed an experimental Ridge Regression model to investigate whether pre-monsoon rainfall and soil moisture can help explain subsequent monsoon rainfall. Its performance is evaluated using chronological historical backtesting and comparison with a historical-average baseline.

The future outlook provides exploratory statistical projections based on historical rainfall patterns. These are not operational weather forecasts or official flood warnings.

What benefits does it provide?

FloodLens makes complex Earth-observation datasets easier to explore and understand. It helps users identify rainfall patterns, compare regions, examine long-term environmental changes, and understand the relationship between rainfall, soil moisture, and geographical conditions. It also provides transparent methods, visual evidence, and data-source information that can support education and further research.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to improve awareness and understanding of changing environmental patterns in Pakistan. By making satellite-based information accessible through an interactive platform, FloodLens can support students, educators, researchers, and environmental analysts in exploring Earth-system changes. In the longer term, we hope to expand its geographical coverage, incorporate additional environmental indicators, and improve its analytical capabilities.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed FloodLens using Python and Streamlit. Our main tools and technologies include:

  • Data sources: NASA GPM IMERG, TerraClimate, and geographical/elevation datasets.
  • Data processing: Python, Pandas, and Xarray.
  • Geospatial data access: Google Earth Engine.
  • Statistical analysis: Mann–Kendall testing, Sen’s slope, Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall testing, and False Discovery Rate correction.
  • Machine learning: Scikit-learn and Ridge Regression.
  • Visualisation and interface: Streamlit and Plotly.
  • Development and deployment: GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud.

The project was developed as a software-based platform and did not require specialised hardware.

How is the project creative and innovative?

FloodLens combines satellite-based rainfall observations, climate variables, statistical trend detection, geographical context, and an experimental machine-learning approach in one interactive platform. Rather than presenting rainfall data as isolated numbers, it allows users to explore where patterns are changing, how large those changes may be, and how confidently they can be interpreted.

An important feature is its emphasis on scientific transparency: it distinguishes statistically significant trends from uncertain patterns, compares the experimental model with a simple baseline, and communicates the limitations of future projections. This helps users explore environmental change without confusing historical analysis with guaranteed predictions.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered data availability, scientific reliability, geographical coverage, spatial resolution, statistical significance, model performance, usability, and transparency. We also considered the limitations of satellite and climate datasets, differences between regional rainfall patterns, and the risk of overstating what a statistical model can predict.

We designed FloodLens to be accessible through a web browser, understandable to non-specialists, and useful for further exploration of Pakistan’s changing rainfall patterns.
